name: Kalabari-Ijo
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Harry, Otelemate G. 2003. Kalabari-Ijo (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 33(1): 113-120. doi:10.1017/S002510030300121X (Cambridge Core open PDF).
catalog_quote: Kalab.ari. is a tone language with two tone levels, high, / !/ and low, / Ÿ/. In addition, a phonemic downstep, [Õ !], occurs, which can give rise to a three-way contrast in morphemes, for example, /ı́kú/ 'lice' /ı́Õkú/ 'heavy' /ı́kù/ 'cocoyam' Further, downdrift occurs in Kalab.ari., whereby in an utterance any successive high tone is on a pitch lower than a preceding high due to an assimilatory effect of a surface intervening low tone (Jenewari 1977, Harry 1998). Similarly, downstep is underlyingly a high tone lowered by a preceding unassociated low tone in Kalab.ari.. All tones will be marked in broad and narrow transcriptions of the illustrative passage. In the orthographic rendition of the passage, high tone will be marked with the acute accent, downstep with a macron and low tone left unmarked, following the present orthographic conventions for Kalab.ari. (Jenewari 1978).

new_statements.quote: Kalabari has a basic contrast between low (L) and high (H) tone. Downstepped high tones (i.e. ꜜH) also occur in some underlying and derived contexts, discussed separately in §2.4. All lexical morphemes and most functional morphemes are fully specified for tone on all tone-bearing units.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record for kala1381 is classification tonal, rule empty, deciding quote from Harry 2003 (JIPA): 'Kalabari is a tone language with two tone levels, high and low.' Rolle & Harry 2025 says the same (L/H contrast, downstep) and adds nothing on word stress, so it agrees with the tonal classification and leaves the stress rule empty.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kalabari is described as a two-tone language (L vs H, plus downstepped H in some contexts) with every lexical morpheme fully specified for tone; the paper contains no statement about word stress in Kalabari. The word 'stress' occurs only in cross-linguistic asides on pp. 17-18 (stress-tone affinity in other languages, de Lacy 2002 prominence hierarchy) and in reference titles.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; the paper's topic is low-tone spread from three monosyllabic onsetless low-toned V-clitics, which it treats as prosodically deficient (not independent phonological words), pp. 17-18.
new_statements.identity_note: Rolle & Harry 2025, p. 3: 'The data for this paper is based around the speech and intuitions of the second author, a speaker of the Buguma dialect (also called Asarị)', Kalabari [ijn], Ijoid, far south of Nigeria (Niger Delta), roughly 500,000 speakers. Akinlabi 1997 was not opened, so its variety is unknown.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the Cambridge Core text we hold layer of Harry 2003 at pp.118-119 'Tone system'; the article never uses the word 'stress'. (2) Deciding source is a 2003 JIPA Illustration by the language's principal phonologist; held corroboration from Harry & Hyman 2014 (H vs L lexical tones + downstep, construction-assigned phrasal melodies; 'stress' only in typological contrasts) and newly downloaded Rolle & Harry 2025 PDA (p.4: basic L/H contrast + downstepped H, all morphemes fully specified for tone; no Kalabari stress rule). (3) The one materially fuller source, Harry 2004 CSLI tone monograph, is not open (publisher page checked; e-book ISBN only) and by all citing summaries describes the same H/L+downstep system; Jenewari 1977/1980 are print-only and older.
